answers.gloss: The transport circuit that an IP/VPN service is bound to ride over. Cascade consumes it as an externally owned transport-domain resource; the concept denotes that circuit in its role as the service underlay, not a separate packet service.
answers.relations: It carries c.service; conversely, c.service rides it. Its lifecycle and transport realization are owned outside Cascade.

answers.gloss: A logical service attachment where the IP/VPN service meets a customer router at a site; it is not itself the physical transport demarcation.
answers.example: att-NY-SVC42 is the New York attachment of SVC-42.
answers.relations: It belongs to c.service and bears c.vlan encapsulation. A service can have multiple attachments.

answers.gloss: The committed information rate guaranteed end to end to the service's customer traffic, rather than a physical bearer capacity or merely a local access policer setting.
answers.example: SVC-42 has a CIR of 5 Gbit/s.
answers.relations: It is an attribute of c.service. The service's underlay must have sufficient transport capacity to support it, but c.rate is not the underlay's raw line rate.

answers.gloss: A promised service-level latency commitment represented by a named SLA tier, not an observed measurement or raw transport metric. The model does not independently specify whether the threshold is one-way or round-trip; that is defined by the tier policy.
answers.example: SVC-42 uses latency tier T2, whose policy threshold is at most 8 ms.
answers.relations: It is an SLA attribute of c.service and constrains the transport underlay selected for that service.

answers.gloss: The service's resilience requirement that connectivity survive a failure in its transport path. It is expressed at the IP-service intent layer but is expected to be fulfilled by transport diversity or protection below it.
answers.example: SVC-42 must remain connected after one underlay path failure.
answers.relations: It is an attribute of c.service and constrains how c.underlay is provided. It concerns transport-path failure survivability, not an IP routing protocol object.

answers.gloss: The IP class of service applied to customer traffic, governing router scheduling and drop priority; it is not a transport restoration or protection grade.
answers.example: SVC-42 uses gold class, mapped to a low-latency router queue.
answers.relations: It is an attribute of c.service and affects packet treatment in the IP layer.

answers.gloss: The customer-facing Ethernet VLAN tag that identifies traffic on a service attachment; it is a packet/Ethernet encapsulation object rather than a transport bearer.
answers.example: C-VLAN 100 is configured on SVC-42's New York attachment.
answers.relations: It is borne on c.attachment. Different service attachments may have their own VLAN identifiers.

answers.gloss: The end-to-end IP/VPN service delivered to a customer. It rides a transport underlay but is not itself known as a service object in the transport domain, which sees the supporting circuit.
answers.example: SVC-42 is a point-to-point IP service from New York to Frankfurt.
answers.relations: It rides c.underlay and terminates logically at c.attachment objects. c.rate, c.latency, c.protection, and c.grade are service attributes; c.vlan identifies customer traffic on each attachment.

answers.gloss: A provisioned transport-domain circuit carrying a client end to end across the optical core. It is the underlay resource on which an external IP/VPN service can ride.
answers.example: CIR-7 runs from the New York hand-off to the Frankfurt hand-off and supports an external service.
answers.relations: It presents at m.handoff endpoints and is carried on m.bearer resources. The decisive experiment has confirmed identity with c.underlay, including endpoint, capacity, connectivity, and layer role.

answers.gloss: The physical demarcation where a transport circuit presents to client equipment; it is not a logical IP/VPN service attachment.
answers.example: The New York hand-off port where CIR-7 meets the customer router.
answers.relations: It is a physical endpoint on m.circuit. A logical service attachment may ultimately use equipment at that location, but it is not the same modeled object.

answers.gloss: The committed client payload rate that the transport circuit guarantees end to end, excluding the physical bearer's raw line rate.
answers.example: CIR-7 guarantees 5 Gbit/s of committed client payload.
answers.relations: It is an attribute of m.circuit. It describes circuit-level committed capacity, while m.bearer may have a different and larger optical line rate.

answers.gloss: The measured numeric one-way propagation delay of a transport circuit, determined principally by its realized path length; it is not an SLA tier.
answers.example: CIR-7's primary path has a measured one-way latency of 7.2 ms.
answers.relations: It is a measured attribute of m.circuit and its realized transport path.

answers.gloss: Realized transport-layer protection of a circuit against path failures such as a fiber cut or bearer loss, implemented by switching to a diverse path.
answers.example: CIR-7 uses 1+1 path protection and switches away from its primary fiber after a cut.
answers.relations: It is an attribute of m.circuit and describes actual transport behavior, rather than merely a customer service-layer resilience requirement.

answers.gloss: The transport quality grade of a circuit, classifying its physical protection and restoration treatment rather than packet scheduling or drop priority.
answers.example: CIR-7 is platinum grade because it is dual-path protected.
answers.relations: It is an attribute of m.circuit and summarizes transport protection/restoration class; example values include platinum, gold, and best-effort.

answers.gloss: A physical optical bearer, such as a wavelength on fiber, that carries transport circuits. It is internal to the transport domain and has no direct client-facing service meaning.
answers.example: The 193.1 THz wavelength on the New York–Frankfurt span carries CIR-7.
answers.relations: It carries m.circuit and supplies physical optical capacity beneath it; it is distinct from the client-facing circuit itself.
